newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Thailand rate squeeze seen hurting baht.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Thailand rate squeeze seen hurting baht.

text.p: Last week's downgrade of Thailand's foreign currency debt rating was yet more bad news for a battered economy, and experts warned there is little on the horizon to lift investors' spirits.
The decision by Moody's Investors Service last week to cut Thailand's long-term debt ratings to A3 from A2 has raised the nation's borrowing costs and added to an interest rate squeeze.

Caught between rising U.S. interest rates, a strong U.S. dollar and a beleaguered banking sector, Thailand continues to confront an economic outlook that some analysts said inevitably would require a weaker currency.
However, it is depreciation, not devaluation, that is forecast for the Thai baht, one of Asia's most vulnerable currencies after nearly a year of speculative pressure.
"That's the big question, the currency," said Willem Appel, assistant director at ING Barings.

"If they can increase exports sufficiently they should have a relatively stable currency. I'm not so afraid of devaluation. What will probably happen is a continued depreciation, something similar to what Indonesia has experienced," he said.
Thailand has been steadily reducing its targeted value for the baht which, like the Indonesian rupiah, is linked to a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.
On Friday, the baht was fixed at a 10-1/2-year low of 26.10 against the U.S. dollar, which keeps on gaining against the Japanese yen and German mark.
Thailand's currency link also requires interest rates to rise in line with those in the United States, which are becoming subject to increased pressure on strong inflation data.

Thailand has already experienced some interest rate spread contraction against the United States following last month's 25-basis point increase in the Federal funds rate, but analysts said the downgrade was sufficiently anticipated to ward off capital flight.
It has, however, raised concern about longer-term monetary policy in Thailand, which had hoped to cut rates later this year in a bid to boost competitiveness.
"The Bank of Thailand may have to adjust rates upwards. With the Thai baht at 26.07, that means Thai rates have to move up," said James Wilson, assistant director, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Real interest rates of about five percent remain sufficiently attractive to fund the nation's current account deficit, said economist Peter van DerShaft at ING Barings.
"They need to maintain these rates to finance the current account deficit and of course, defend the baht, but it's more a question of funding the current account deficit," he said.

Higher rates, however, will hammer the nation's cash-strapped banking sector and force more finance companies and banks into the market to raise funds. Wilson warned that a number of rights issues are planned and this will pressure a stock market believed to be bottoming out between 675 and 725.
A spate of bad corporate earnings for banks will also dampen stock market sentiment until September, as would any further ratings downgrade by Moody's or any other agency.
Opinion was divided over whether this was likely.

Van DerShaft argued that the Moody's downgrade came in response to factors already well-known by the market, and an improving trade balance -- albeit a function of higher imports rather than exports -- offers a glimmer of hope.

"What they are doing now is what they should be doing to narrow the current account deficit," he said. "We are seeing a slowdown in growth, but it's not a meltdown...This is not a situation that is unmanageable."
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6470
